editorial:
Imagine spending your days at a capsule hotel where the guests are just as strange as the rooms. You will meet Nitobe, a guy who loves reading philosophy and looking at crabs, and his buddy Sakamoto, who is unfortunately obsessed with ending his own life. The movie feels like a series of small snapshots. You see a grieving mother from Finland and a woman on the run, all staying in these tiny plastic pods. It is a slow, quiet experience that makes you think about how we all live side by side in a big city without ever really knowing the people next to us.

What really works here is the calm acting and the weird, funny conversations between the two main friends. It does not have a big plot or loud action, which might bore some people, but it is perfect if you want something relaxing. If you enjoy these kinds of quiet stories, you should definitely try renting it on Apple TV or adding the 4K Blu-ray to your physical collection for the best picture quality. It is a great pick for a rainy Sunday when you just want to zone out and reflect on life.
endingExplained: The movie does not have a big twist or a happy ending where everyone becomes friends. Instead, it ends by showing that these people continue to exist in their own little bubbles. Nitobe and Sakamoto keep working their jobs, and the guests eventually leave. It wraps up by reminding you that life is mostly made of these tiny, unconnected moments. You realize that even though they never truly bonded, they shared the same space and time.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves slow cinema and character studies.
